newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS SPOTLIGHT-KIEFER FOLLOWS BECKER ROUTE TO TOP.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS SPOTLIGHT-KIEFER FOLLOWS BECKER ROUTE TO TOP.

text.p: Where have we heard this before? Teenage German bursts onto the scene at Wimbledon with no warning, beating a succession of higher-ranked opponents on his way to the last eight. It is enough to make Boris Becker wince.

Those looking to cast 19-year-old Nicolas Kiefer as the 'new Becker' should, however, tread warily. The youngster may be a founder member of the recently-created Becker junior team in Germany, but the cloning laboratory has singularly failed to fashion a 'Boom-Boom' replica.

Slightly-built with a goatee beard, the manner of Kiefer's shock 6-2 7-5 6-2 6-1 victory over world number three Yevgeny Kafelnikov on Tuesday was about as far removed from the 1985 Becker blueprint as it is possible to get.

The crop-haired German is not one of those big-serving giants who tend to spring to prominence on grass, but instead a quick-witted competitor with fast hands and more than a hint of the Andre Agassi about his short-striding walk and precise passing shots.

In between the showers which delayed his success, Kiefer also displayed a mental strength which Becker would at least recognise and approve of. A code violation for swearing and smashing a ball out of the court failed to stop him winning a tight second set, and he had to display further inner steel following lengthy injury treatment in the fourth set.

Kiefer spent several minutes flat out on the grass while a trainer worked hard to alleviate stiffness in his lower back, yet responded by breaking Kafelnikov in the very next game for 2-0 in the fourth set, arguably the match's decisive passage of play.
It was all pretty impressive stuff from someone who only officially finished high school last Monday, but those who have charted his progress through the junior ranks are unsurprised.
A former junior champion at both the U.S. Open and the Australian Open in 1995, he also reached the boy's final at Wimbledon the same year only to lose 6-2 6-2 to Olivier Mutis of France.

Plenty of juniors lose their way en route to the senior tour -- Mutis is currently ranked 476th on the ATP computer compared to Kiefer's position of 98th -- but the German appears to be one of those who flourish in better company.

Australian Mark Philippoussis, a losing finalist at 1994 junior Wimbledon who has subsequently risen to 13th in the world inside three years, is an obvious role model and Kiefer is already showing a steady improvement.

He reached the semifinals in Milan at the beginning of March and took Kafelnikov to two tiebreaks when the pair met on grass in Halle last month, benefiting from tactical advice from Becker who offers him tips on how best to approach his various opponents.
"He tells me how to play against players...I speak to him every day," confirmed Kiefer.

If he can get past Australian Todd Woodbridge and reach the semifinals on Friday, on the eve of his 20th birthday, he may encounter Becker on the opposite side of the net. It might put fatal strain on the master-pupil relationship, but would provide the acid test of the apprentice's mettle.
"It seems funny to have a pupil in the quarter-finals with me," said Becker, impressed by Kiefer's hand-eye co-ordination the moment he saw him.
He may not find it so amusing if his protege's dreams interfere with his own.
